narrative:
The model determined that you have a 75.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the second decile, noticeably lower than the average ranking of accepted students. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; you stood in the third decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth. These two early indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates carried more weight than any other information the model considered.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 29.3 it is below the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model still treated the score itself as mildly encouraging compared with the rest of your profile.

Taken together, the model saw your lower class rankings as strong signals that you would struggle to pass the bar on the first try. To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score before reapplying.
